---
description: "Use when selecting, researching, reporting, or charting project cohorts for AI-policy coverage, including ecosyste.ms Critical dependencies."
applyTo: "reports/**"
---
# Project cohort policy analysis

- Keep each cohort separate, with its own landing page, project reports, and visual summaries. A cohort index should explain its selection method and link to source reports and charts.
- Keep landing-page text brief and non-redundant. Use bullets only when they make separate criteria easier to compare; prose may be clearer when ideas depend on each other. Review clarity rather than assuming a format is clearer.
- If the requested cohort is the top N projects **with AI policies**, continue down the stated ranking until N projects with an explicit AI-related policy are verified. Do not equate the top N ranked repositories with the top N that have policies, and do not count a generic contribution guide as an AI policy.
- Search beyond README files. Inspect repository trees and policy-bearing document types represented in the CHAOSS cohort summaries: policy documents, contribution guides, codes of conduct, `AGENTS.md`/agent guidance, pull-request templates, READMEs, FAQs, and other relevant official project documents. Check root, `docs/`, and hidden `.github/` paths. Use social posts only when explicitly in scope and no more authoritative source is available.
- Treat a project as having a qualifying AI policy only when an official source contains an explicit AI-related rule, requirement, permission, restriction, or guidance. Record exactly which documents were reviewed; a missing rule in one document is not evidence that the whole project has no policy.
- Cite each finding to the source document, preferably a stable line link or revision. Preserve scope and qualifications; do not turn a restriction on one submission type, workflow, contributor group, or security-report process into a project-wide code-contribution ban.
- Verify every indexed file against its contents, not just its filename or a link from another document. Distinguish substantive rules, explicit policy references, security-report-only wording, and agent-specific instructions; exclude generic agent guidance with no AI-related rule. Record the role of references and agent instructions so readers do not mistake them for general policy.
- Check repository redirects and owner changes against the cohort's retrieval-time mapping. Keep historical selection decisions explicit, and disclose when a later move creates a current-owner overlap.
- Put source wording in quotation marks only when it is a verified direct quote, preserving its wording. Link the quote to its source and line. Label interpretations as summaries, use neutral language, and do not present invented labels or paraphrases as source terminology. In particular, phrases such as “AI slop” must be quoted only if those exact words occur in the linked source.
- Follow the existing CHAOSS report format and terminology (nine CHAOSS domains plus the project's tenth domain, slop, which records negative or dismissive wording about AI as the project's own words). Use `reports/chaoss_list_of_projects/` for the established CHAOSS cohort and keep new cohorts in their own `reports/<cohort>/` folders.
- For ranked cohorts, record the feed endpoint, ranking field and order, retrieval date, package-to-repository mapping, rank, and source count. Keep index, report, and chart values in agreement.
- Build ranked "top N with AI policies" cohorts this way (as in `reports/critical-dependencies/`):
  1. Pull enough feed pages to reach N qualifiers, map packages to GitHub repositories, and count a repository once at its highest-ranked package. Report positions among distinct repositories, not package record numbers.
  2. Scan every repository down the ranking: list the file tree, read all documentation-type files at the root and in `docs/`, `doc/`, `.github/` and agent-config folders, and search them for AI terms (AI, LLM, large language model, ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude, Gemini, Codex, Cursor, generative, agentic, autonomous agent, machine-generated). Read every match by hand; do not trust the regex.
  3. Skip repositories without an explicit AI-related rule and do not report them as findings. List false positives and excluded matches (changelog entries, generic agent-instruction files with no AI-related rule, meeting notes, name collisions) with the reason, in a "Reviewed and excluded" section.
  4. Apply one project per GitHub owner. When an owner has several qualifiers, show the one with the most substantive AI language, with feed position as the tie-break, and say how many same-owner repositories were left out. Only quote counts you computed from hand-reviewed data; label automated counts as approximate.
  5. Separate security-report-only AI wording (for example a sentence in `SECURITY.md`) from project-wide policy. Include it only as scoped, leave the nine rule domains blank for it, and mark it distinctly in tables and charts.
  6. State coverage limits in the landing page: paths nested deeper than one level, organization-level `.github` repositories, websites, wikis and social posts were not read, and name any known policy that lives only there.
- Every cohort needs three chart views, as SVG with title, desc and alt text, kept in agreement with the tables: a ranked bar chart of the project metric, a document-type grouping chart labelled by the exact file names where AI policy was found (for example `SECURITY.md, security.md`, `AI_POLICY.md, ai-policy.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md, contributing.md`, `AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md`, `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md, ISSUE_TEMPLATE/*`, `README.md`; never descriptive names alone, so a reader can check each file; a project counts once per file name), and policy coverage by domain as a bar chart plus a pie chart (`X` or `~` entries count; one report can count in several domains). Add a by-file-name table that lists each project once per file name, with the project name linked to the exact file (add further links for extra files in the same group; do not repeat the file name beside the project), and a coverage-by-domain table to the landing page. Name actual files, not descriptions, in charts and tables so findings can be validated.
- The tenth domain, slop, records wording in the project's own text that is negative or dismissive of AI or its output. Mark it `X` with a verified quote and leave supervision, scope and accountability blank. Neutral quality language ("low-quality AI content will be closed") is not slop. Search each cohort's AI documents for such terms and read every match. Pre-slop CHAOSS list reports are not re-scored; say so rather than showing blanks.
- Before finishing, validate cohort size and qualification, report-to-index links, all relative Markdown links, SVG XML, chart labels against source data, every direct quote against the live source (quotes must sit within a single line), and `git diff --check`.
- For the Critical dependencies cohort, run `python scripts/check_critical_dependency_sources.py` to reconcile report source paths, the by-file index, counts, and chart description. Keep regression checks for known edge cases such as linked-only policy references, AI-specific agent instructions, unrelated `AGENTS.md` files, and renamed repositories.
